quote: Adults should do at least 150–300 min of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or at least 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of moderate-intensity and vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week for substantial health benefits
claim: Adults (18-64, including those with chronic conditions or disability) should accumulate 150-300 min/week of moderate-intensity or 75-150 min/week of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, or an equivalent combination (strong recommendation).

quote: Adults should also do muscle-strengthening activities at moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week, as these provide additional health benefits.
claim: Adults should also do moderate-or-greater-intensity muscle-strengthening activity for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days per week.

quote: For all populations, doing some physical activity is better than doing none. If individuals are not currently meeting these recommendations, doing some physical activity will bring benefits to health. Individuals should start with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increase frequency, intensity and duration over time.
claim: Some activity is better than none: people below the recommendations still benefit, and should start with small amounts and increase frequency, then duration and intensity, gradually.
used_for: starting dose for inactive people; messaging

quote: Pre-exercise medical clearance is generally unnecessary for individuals without contraindications prior to beginning light-intensity or moderate-intensity physical activity not exceeding the demands of brisk walking or everyday living.
claim: Medical clearance is generally not needed before starting light- or moderate-intensity activity (up to brisk walking) in people without contraindications.
caveat: Formal pre-participation screening (PAR-Q+) is covered by the SAF cluster.

quote: An individual who is habitually engaging in moderate-intensity activity can gradually increase to vigorous intensity activity without needing to consult a healthcare provider. Those who develop new symptoms when increasing their levels of activity should consult a healthcare provider.
claim: People already doing regular moderate activity can progress gradually to vigorous activity without consulting a clinician; anyone who develops new symptoms while increasing activity should see a healthcare provider.
used_for: progression to vigorous; referral on new symptoms

quote: Adults should limit the amount of time spent being sedentary. Replacing sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity (including light intensity) provides health benefits;To help reduce the detrimental effects of high levels of sedentary behaviour on health, adults should aim to do more than the recommended levels of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
claim: Adults should limit sedentary time; replacing it with activity of any intensity helps, and very sedentary adults should aim above the minimum MVPA target.

quote: there was insufficient evidence to specify quantitative thresholds of sedentary behaviour
claim: WHO found insufficient evidence to set a numeric upper limit on sedentary time for adults.

quote: older adults should do varied multicomponent physical activity that emphasises functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on 3 or more days a week, to enhance functional capacity and to prevent falls.
claim: Adults 65+ should, within their weekly activity, do varied multicomponent activity emphasising functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on 3 or more days per week to prevent falls.
population: older adults 65+, including those with chronic conditions or disability

quote: Children and adolescents should do at least an average of 60 min/day of moderate-to-vigorous intensity, mostly aerobic, physical activity, across the week;Vigorous-intensity aerobic activities, as well as those that strengthen muscle and bone should be incorporated at least 3 days a week.
claim: Children and adolescents (5-17) should average at least 60 min/day of mostly aerobic MVPA across the week, with vigorous aerobic and muscle- and bone-strengthening activities on at least 3 days per week.

quote: Pregnant women considering athletic competition or exercising significantly above the recommended guidelines should seek supervision from a specialist healthcare provider;Pregnant women should be informed by their healthcare provider of the danger signs for when to stop, or limit physical activity and to consult a qualified healthcare provider immediately if they occur.
claim: Pregnant athletes or women training well above the guideline should be supervised by a specialist healthcare provider; danger signs require stopping and immediate consultation.

quote: Adults with chronic conditions may wish to consult with a physical activity specialist or healthcare professional for advice on the types and amounts of activity appropriate for their individual needs, abilities, functional limitations/complications, medications and overall treatment plan.
claim: Adults with chronic conditions should aim for the guideline as able, and may need a healthcare professional's advice on types and amounts of activity given complications, medications and treatment plan.

quote: These guidelines are for the general population and do not address the benefits and harms experienced by athletes undertaking the types and amounts of activity necessary to improve performance-related fitness for participation in competition.
claim: The WHO doses are public-health minimums for the general population, not training prescriptions for competitive athletes.

quote: Adults who do not yet do the equivalent of 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week (inactive or insufficiently active) should work gradually toward this goal. The initial amount of activity should be at a light or moderate intensity, for short periods of time, with the sessions spread throughout the week.
claim: Inactive adults should work gradually toward 150 min/week, starting with light or moderate intensity, short sessions spread through the week.
used_for: starting dose for the sedentary adult

quote: Initially, these activities can be done just 1 day a week starting at a light or moderate level of effort. Over time, the number of days a week can be increased to 2, and then possibly to more than 2. Each week, the intensity can be increased slightly until it becomes moderate or greater.
claim: Muscle strengthening for inactive adults can start at 1 day/week at light-moderate effort, then 2 days and possibly more, raising intensity slightly each week until moderate or greater.

quote: Generally, start with relatively moderate-intensity activity. Avoid relatively vigorous-intensity activity, such as shoveling heavy snow or running. Adults with low fitness may need to start with light activity, or a mix of light- to moderate-intensity activity. ... First, increase the number of minutes per session (duration) and the number of days a week (frequency) of moderate-intensity activity. Later, if desired, increase the intensity.
claim: Inactive adults should start at relatively moderate intensity (light if fitness is low), avoid relatively vigorous activity such as running at first, increase duration and frequency before intensity.
population: inactive adults and those with low activity

quote: Pay attention to the relative size of the increase in physical activity each week, as this is related to injury risk. For example, a 20-minute increase each week is safer for a person who already does 200 minutes a week of jogging (a 10% increase) than in a person who does 40 minutes a week (a 50% increase).
claim: Injury risk relates to the relative size of the weekly increase: +20 min is 10% for someone doing 200 min/week but 50% for someone doing 40 min/week.
caveat: Illustrative example, not a validated '10% rule'; running-specific progression evidence belongs to the END cluster.

quote: adding a small and comfortable amount of light- to moderate-intensity activity, such as walking 5 to 15 minutes per session, 2 to 3 times a week, to one’s usual activities results in a low risk of musculoskeletal injury and no known risk of severe cardiac events.
claim: Adding 5-15 minutes of walking per session, 2-3 times per week, to usual activity carries a low risk of musculoskeletal injury and no known risk of severe cardiac events.

quote: Youth and young adults probably can safely increase activity by small amounts every week or two. Older adults appear to require more time to adapt to a new level of activity, in the range of 2 to 4 weeks.
claim: Young people can probably increase activity in small steps every 1-2 weeks; older adults appear to need 2-4 weeks to adapt to each new level.
number_note: 'every week or two' is written in words in the source; 2-4 weeks is quoted.

quote: The ACSM recommends that most adults engage in moderate-intensity cardiorespiratory exercise training for ≥30 min·d on ≥5 d·wk for a total of ≥150 min·wk, vigorous-intensity cardiorespiratory exercise training for ≥20 min·d on ≥3 d·wk (≥75 min·wk), or a combination
claim: ACSM: most adults should do moderate cardiorespiratory exercise at least 30 min/day on at least 5 days (at least 150 min/week) or vigorous exercise at least 20 min/day on at least 3 days (at least 75 min/week), or a combination.
number: >=30 min/day on >=5 days (>=150 min/week); >=20 min/day on >=3 days (>=75 min/week)

quote: On 2-3 d·wk, adults should also perform resistance exercises for each of the major muscle groups, and neuromotor exercise involving balance, agility, and coordination. Crucial to maintaining joint range of movement, completing a series of flexibility exercises for each the major muscle-tendon groups (a total of 60 s per exercise) on ≥2 d·wk is recommended.
claim: ACSM: resistance exercise for each major muscle group and neuromotor (balance, agility, coordination) exercise on 2-3 days/week; flexibility exercises for each major muscle-tendon group, 60 s total per exercise, on at least 2 days/week.

quote: Educating adults about and screening for signs and symptoms of CHD and gradual progression of exercise intensity and volume may reduce the risks of exercise. Consultations with a medical professional and diagnostic exercise testing for CHD are useful when clinically indicated but are not recommended for universal screening to enhance the safety of exercise.
claim: Educating about coronary symptoms and progressing intensity and volume gradually may reduce exercise risk; medical consultation and exercise testing are for clinical indications, not universal screening.

quote: it is recommended that resistance training programmes be performed 2–3 times per week, starting with 1–2 sets and progressing to 2–3 sets of 8–12 repetitions.
claim: Older adults: resistance training 2-3 times per week, starting with 1-2 sets and progressing to 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions, targeting major muscle groups used in daily function.
number: 2-3 times/week; 1-2 sets to 2-3 sets of 8-12 reps

quote: Start at 30–40% of 1RM and progress to heavier loads of 70–80% 1 RM
claim: Older adults: start resistance training at 30-40% of 1RM and progress to 70-80% of 1RM.

quote: Whilst the absolute loads that can be lifted may be very low initially, even extreme frailty is not a contraindication to robust exercise. Indeed, frailty is one of the most crucial reasons to prescribe an exercise regimen.
claim: Frailty is not a contraindication to resistance exercise; it is a key reason to prescribe it, with low absolute loads at first.
caveat: In practice, frail clients should be trained with clinical oversight or by qualified staff; see referral rules.

quote: Older adults with disabilities may need more direct supervision when performing muscle-strengthening activities than those who are more robust. Caution should be taken, especially during the first phase of an exercise program, because even a small injury may require weeks to recover
claim: Older adults with disabilities may need more direct supervision; be cautious in the first phase because even a small injury can take weeks to recover from.

quote: The endurance exercises may start with a duration of 5–10 min in the first weeks of training, progressing to 15–30 min for the remainder of the program, with frequencies from 3 to 7 days per week.
claim: Older adults: endurance sessions can start at 5-10 min in the first weeks and progress to 15-30 min, 3-7 days per week.

quote: We recommend exercise programmes for fall prevention for community-dwelling older adults which include balance challenging and functional exercises (e.g. sit-to-stand, stepping), with sessions three times or more weekly which are individualised, progressed in intensity for at least 12 weeks and continued longer for greater effect.
claim: Falls prevention: balance-challenging and functional exercise (sit-to-stand, stepping), three or more sessions weekly, individualised, progressed for at least 12 weeks and continued longer (GRADE 1A).
number: three or more sessions/week; at least 12 weeks

quote: An adult who sustains an injury requiring medical (including surgical) treatment, reports recurrent falls (≥2) in the previous 12 months, was laying on the floor unable to rise independently for at least one hour, is considered frail or is suspected to have experienced a transient loss of consciousness should be regarded as at high risk of future falls.
claim: High falls risk: a fall with injury needing medical treatment, 2 or more falls in 12 months, lying on the floor unable to get up for at least an hour, frailty, or suspected transient loss of consciousness.

quote: Older adults who had a single non-severe fall but also have gait and or balance problems, should be considered as being at ‘intermediate risk’ and would benefit from a strength and balance exercise intervention
claim: One non-severe fall plus gait or balance problems is intermediate risk; strength and balance training is the indicated intervention.
used_for: who the coach can train directly

quote: These high-risk older adults should be offered a multifactorial falls risk assessment. Suspicion of a syncopal fall should trigger syncope evaluation and management.
claim: High-risk older adults should get a multifactorial falls risk assessment by clinicians; a suspected syncopal fall needs syncope evaluation.
population: older adults at high falls risk

quote: The FP includes 5 criteria: slow gait speed, low physical activity, unintentional weight loss, exhaustion and muscle weakness; where ≥3 components categorises an individual as ‘frail’, 1 or 2 as prefrail
claim: Frailty phenotype: slow gait, low activity, unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness; 3 or more criteria = frail, 1-2 = prefrail.
used_for: recognising frailty / weight loss as a flag

quote: Exercise reduces the rate of falls by 23% (rate ratio (RaR) 0.77, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.71 to 0.83; 12,981 participants, 59 studies; high-certainty evidence).
claim: Exercise reduces the rate of falls in community-dwelling older people by 23% (RaR 0.77, 95% CI 0.71-0.83; high certainty).

quote: Multiple types of exercise (most commonly balance and functional exercises plus resistance exercises) probably reduce the rate of falls by 34% (RaR 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88; 1374 participants, 11 studies; moderate-certainty evidence)
claim: Multicomponent programmes (balance/functional plus resistance) probably reduce the fall rate by 34% (moderate certainty).

quote: We are uncertain of the effects of programmes that are primarily resistance training, or dance or walking programmes on the rate of falls and the number of people who experience falls.
claim: Programmes that are mainly resistance training, dance or walking have uncertain effects on falls; balance work must be included.
used_for: do not rely on walking or lifting alone for falls

quote: Pregnant women should accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week to achieve clinically meaningful health benefits and reductions in pregnancy complications.
claim: Pregnant women without contraindications should accumulate at least 150 min/week of moderate-intensity activity.

quote: Pelvic floor muscle training (e.g., Kegel exercises) may be performed on a daily basis to reduce the risk of urinary incontinence. Instruction in proper technique is recommended to obtain optimal benefits.
claim: Daily pelvic floor muscle training may reduce urinary incontinence risk; technique instruction is recommended.

quote: Women with absolute contraindications may continue their usual activities of daily living but should not participate in more strenuous activities. Women with relative contraindications should discuss the advantages and disadvantages of moderate-to-vigorous intensity physical activity with their obstetric care provider prior to participation.
claim: Absolute contraindication: only usual daily activities, no strenuous exercise. Relative contraindication: discuss MVPA with the obstetric care provider before taking part.

quote: Absolute contraindications to exercise are the following: ruptured membranes, premature labour, unexplained persistent vaginal bleeding, placenta previa after 28 weeks gestation, preeclampsia, incompetent cervix, intrauterine growth restriction, high-order multiple pregnancy (e.g., triplets), uncontrolled Type I diabetes, uncontrolled hypertension, uncontrolled thyroid disease, other serious cardiovascular, respiratory or systemic disorder.
claim: Absolute contraindications in pregnancy include ruptured membranes, premature labour, unexplained persistent vaginal bleeding, placenta previa after 28 weeks, preeclampsia, incompetent cervix, growth restriction, triplets or more, uncontrolled type 1 diabetes, hypertension or thyroid disease, and other serious cardiovascular, respiratory or systemic disorders.

quote: Relative contraindications to exercise are the following: recurrent pregnancy loss, gestational hypertension, a history of spontaneous preterm birth, mild/moderate cardiovascular or respiratory disease, symptomatic anemia, malnutrition, eating disorder, twin pregnancy after the 28th week, other significant medical conditions.
claim: Relative contraindications in pregnancy include recurrent pregnancy loss, gestational hypertension, previous spontaneous preterm birth, mild/moderate cardiovascular or respiratory disease, symptomatic anaemia, malnutrition, eating disorder, twins after week 28.

quote: In the absence of obstetric or medical complications or contraindications, physical activity in pregnancy is safe and desirable, and pregnant women should be encouraged to continue or to initiate safe physical activities.
claim: ACOG: without obstetric or medical complications, physical activity in pregnancy is safe and desirable; pregnant women should be encouraged to continue or start safe activities.

quote: We recommend accumulating at least 120 minutes of MVPA (e.g., brisk walking, cycling) spread over four or more days of the week that incorporates a variety of aerobic and resistance training activities.
claim: Postpartum (first year): accumulate at least 120 min/week of MVPA over four or more days, mixing aerobic and resistance training.
population: postpartum women, first year, without contraindications

quote: We recommend performing pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) daily to reduce the risk of urinary incontinence and rehabilitate pelvic floor muscles impacted by pregnancy, labour, and/or delivery. Instruction on proper technique from a pelvic floor physiotherapist is recommended to obtain optimal benefits.
claim: Postpartum: daily pelvic floor muscle training, with technique instruction from a pelvic floor physiotherapist.

quote: We suggest initiating early mobilization with light-intensity physical activity (e.g., gentle walking, pelvic floor muscle training) and progressing to MVPA once surgical incisions or perineal tears have sufficiently healed and vaginal bleeding (lochia) does not increase with MVPA.
claim: Postpartum: start with light activity (gentle walking, pelvic floor training) and progress to MVPA once incisions or perineal tears have healed and bleeding does not increase with MVPA.

quote: We suggest following an individualized, gradual, and symptom-based progression toward at least 120 minutes/ week of MVPA.
claim: Postpartum progression should be individualised, gradual and symptom-based (no fixed week-by-week timeline).

quote: Severe abdominal pain Vaginal bleeding not associated with menses Postpartum cardiomyopathy Cesarean section with symptoms that worsen with moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (e.g., surgical incision pain) High blood pressure (>140/90 mmHg systolic/diastolic) that is not stable
claim: Postpartum relative contraindications include severe abdominal pain, non-menstrual vaginal bleeding, postpartum cardiomyopathy, caesarean symptoms worsening with MVPA, and unstable blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg (list continues: eating disorder, malnutrition, possible anaemia/low energy availability, DVT signs, chest pain, dizziness, syncope).

quote: While the following are not contraindications to physical activity, additional screening, support, and treatment for potential barriers to MVPA by a healthcare provider or qualified exercise professional may be recommended: Mental health Pelvic floor and abdominal wall function Musculoskeletal pain Wound healing
claim: Mental health, pelvic floor and abdominal wall function, musculoskeletal pain and wound healing are not contraindications but may need screening or treatment by a healthcare provider or qualified exercise professional.
used_for: when to involve a pelvic-health physio

quote: Current research indicates that resistance training can be a safe, effective and worthwhile activity for children and adolescents provided that qualified professionals supervise all training sessions and provide age-appropriate instruction on proper lifting procedures and safe training guidelines.
claim: Resistance training is safe and effective for children and adolescents when qualified professionals supervise sessions and teach proper technique.
used_for: youth resistance training: allowed with supervision

quote: injury to the growth cartilage has not been reported in any prospective youth resistance training study that provided professional guidance and instruction.17, 25–49 Furthermore, there is no evidence that resistance training will negatively impact growth in height during childhood and adolescence.
claim: No growth-plate injury has been reported in supervised prospective youth resistance-training studies, and there is no evidence that resistance training stunts growth.

quote: The focus of youth resistance training programmes should be on learning proper exercise technique and not on the amount of weight lifted.
claim: Youth programmes should focus on learning technique, not on the load lifted.

quote: Performance-enhancing substances (PESs) are used commonly by children and adolescents in attempts to improve athletic performance. More recent data reveal that these same substances often are used for appearance-related reasons as well.
claim: Adolescents use performance-enhancing substances for performance and often for appearance; 'bulking' goals warrant attention to body image.

quote: Concerns regarding use of legal PESs include high rates of product contamination, correlation with future use of anabolic androgenic steroids, and adverse effects on the focus and experience of youth sports participation.
claim: AAP concerns about legal supplements in youth: frequent contamination, association with later anabolic steroid use, and harm to the youth sport experience.

quote: For most young athletes, PES use does not produce significant gains over those seen with the onset of puberty and adherence to an appropriate nutrition and training program.
claim: For most young athletes, supplements and other PES add little beyond puberty plus sound training and nutrition.

quote: we recommend that creatine supplementation only be considered for use by younger athletes who: a.) are involved in serious/competitive supervised training; b.) are consuming a well-balanced and performance enhancing diet; c.) are knowledgeable about appropriate use of creatine; and d.) do not exceed recommended dosages.
claim: ISSN: creatine may be considered for younger athletes only if in serious supervised training, eating a well-balanced diet, informed about proper use, and not exceeding recommended doses.
caveat: ISSN position differs from the AAP; the coach should not recommend supplements to minors (scope of practice) and should refer to a physician or sports dietitian with parental involvement.

quote: watch for the following warning signs when you exercise. If you have any of them, stop and call your ob-gyn. Bleeding from the vagina Feeling dizzy or faint Shortness of breath before starting exercise Chest pain Headache Muscle weakness Calf pain or swelling Regular, painful contractions of the uterus Fluid gushing or leaking from the vagina
claim: Pregnancy warning signs to stop exercise and contact the obstetric provider: vaginal bleeding, dizziness or faintness, shortness of breath before exercise, chest pain, headache, muscle weakness, calf pain or swelling, regular painful contractions, fluid leaking from the vagina.

quote: Contact sports and sports that put you at risk of getting hit in the abdomen, including ice hockey, boxing, soccer, and basketball Skydiving Activities that may result in a fall, such as downhill snow skiing, water skiing, surfing, off-road cycling, gymnastics, and horseback riding "Hot yoga” or “hot Pilates,” which may cause you to become overheated Scuba diving Activities performed above 6,000 feet (if you do not already live at a high altitude)
claim: Avoid in pregnancy: contact sports and abdominal-impact risk, skydiving, fall-prone activities (downhill skiing, surfing, off-road cycling, gymnastics, riding), hot yoga/Pilates, scuba diving, and activity above 6,000 ft unless living at altitude.
caveat: Off-road cycling and other fall-prone sports matter for the coach's cyclists and trail runners; climbing is not named but carries fall risk; discuss with the obstetric provider.

quote: For most individuals planning to participate in a low- to moderate-intensity PA like brisk walking, no pre-exercise medical evaluation is needed unless symptoms of CVD or microvascular complications are present (1, 96). In adults who are currently sedentary, medical clearance is recommended prior to participation in moderate-to high-intensity PA.
claim: Type 2 diabetes: no medical evaluation is needed before low-to-moderate activity like brisk walking unless CVD symptoms or microvascular complications exist; sedentary adults with T2D should get medical clearance before moderate-to-high-intensity activity.

quote: Individuals managing glycemia with lifestyle improvement alone have minimal risk for hypoglycemia (134). Use of select medications for T2D may increase the risk of exercise-related hypoglycemia, including insulin and insulin secretagogues (i.e., sulfonylureas and meglitinides)
claim: Exercise-related hypoglycaemia risk is minimal with lifestyle management alone but raised with insulin and insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas, meglitinides).
caveat: Medication dose adjustment is outside the coach's scope; refer to the treating clinician.

quote: Particularly for anyone using insulin or taking sulfonylureas (and possibly meglitinides within 2-3 h of physical activity), it is important to carry rapid-acting carbohydrate sources during PA to treat hypoglycemia
claim: People on insulin or sulfonylureas should carry rapid-acting carbohydrate during activity.
population: adults with type 2 diabetes on insulin or secretagogues

quote: Individuals should not begin exercise with a blood glucose >250 mg · dL−1 (13.9 mmol · L−1) if moderate or high levels of blood or urinary ketones are present. Use caution during PA with a blood glucose >300 mg · dL−1 (16.7 mmol · L-1) without excessive ketones, stay hydrated, and only begin if feeling well
claim: Do not start exercise with blood glucose above 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) if ketones are moderate or high; above 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L) without ketones, exercise only with caution, hydrated and feeling well.

quote: Exercise is contraindicated for anyone with unstable or untreated proliferative retinopathy, recent panretinal photocoagulation, or other recent surgical eye treatment.
claim: Exercise is contraindicated with unstable or untreated proliferative retinopathy or after recent eye surgery or laser treatment; with severe retinopathy avoid breath-holding, heavy lifting and head-down positions.

quote: Patients with controlled hypertension can safely participate in low- to moderate-intensity RT with proper breathing techniques.20 Medications can affect hemodynamics, ECG changes, and exercise capacity, and therefore, should be considered when designing RT prescriptions.86 For example, patients taking antihypertensive medications should incorporate extended cooldowns to prevent hypotension.
claim: Controlled hypertension: low-to-moderate-intensity resistance training with proper breathing is safe; people on antihypertensives should use extended cool-downs to prevent hypotension.

quote: adverse signs and symptoms (eg, dizziness, excessive dyspnea, chest pain and pressure, palpitations) require immediate medical evaluation, and patients should discontinue participating in RT until obtaining further medical clearance.
claim: In people with cardiovascular disease, dizziness, excessive breathlessness, chest pain or pressure, or palpitations require immediate medical evaluation and a pause in training until cleared.
population: adults with or at risk of cardiovascular disease

quote: Individuals with implanted pacemakers or defibrillators should consult with their physicians before engaging in upper-body RT.
claim: People with pacemakers or implanted defibrillators should consult their physician before upper-body resistance training.

quote: Do you have a resting blood pressure equal to or greater than 160/90 mmHg with or without medication? (Answer YES if you do not know your resting blood pressure)
claim: PAR-Q+ follow-up: resting blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg or higher (or unknown) in someone with hypertension triggers further evaluation (ePARmed-X+ or qualified professional) before becoming more active.
used_for: BP threshold for referral before progressing
caveat: Screening threshold, not a treatment target; formal screening belongs to SAF.

quote: You are encouraged to start slowly and build up gradually - 20 to 60 minutes of low to moderate intensity exercise, 3-5 days per week including aerobic and muscle strengthening exercises. As you progress, you should aim to accumulate 150 minutes or more of moderate intensity physical activity per week. If you are over the age of 45 yr and NOT accustomed to regular vigorous to maximal effort exercise, consult a qualified exercise professional before engaging in this intensity of exercise.
claim: After a clear PAR-Q+: start with 20-60 min of low-moderate exercise 3-5 days/week, progressing toward 150+ min/week; adults over 45 not used to vigorous exercise should consult a qualified exercise professional before vigorous or maximal efforts.
population: adults who answered no to all PAR-Q+ questions

quote: Overall, there is little evidence of harm, including fractures, occurring while exercising. Furthermore, cases that were identified comprised a mixture of people with and without osteoporosis (as defined by DXA). Exercise is therefore unlikely to cause a fracture
claim: Exercise is unlikely to cause fractures in people with osteoporosis; little evidence of harm exists.

quote: Muscle-strengthening physical activity and exercise is recommended on two or three days of the week to maintain bone strength. [E] For maximum benefit, muscle strengthening should include progressive muscle resistance training. In practice, this is the maximum that can be lifted 8–12 times (building up to three sets for each exercise).
claim: Osteoporosis: progressive resistance training on two or three days per week, building to loads that can be lifted 8-12 times and up to three sets, after learning technique at lower intensity.

quote: Moderate impact exercise is recommended on most days to promote bone strength (eg, stamping, jogging, low-level jumping, hopping) to include at least 50 impacts per session (jogs, hops etc). [C]
claim: Osteoporosis without vertebral or multiple low-trauma fractures: moderate impact (stamping, jogging, low jumps, hops) on most days, at least 50 impacts per session.
population: people with osteoporosis without vertebral fractures

quote: Impact exercise on most days at a level up to brisk walking is recommended, aiming for 150 minutes over the week (20 min per day). This a precautionary measure because of theoretical (unproved) risks of further vertebral fracture in this group. [C] Individualised advice from a physiotherapist is recommended
claim: With vertebral or multiple low-trauma fractures: impact only up to brisk walking (about 150 min/week), and individualised physiotherapist advice for impact and resistance training.
population: people with osteoporosis and vertebral or multiple low-trauma fractures

quote: Movements or exercise that involve sustained, repeated or end-range flexion should be modified or avoided. [C] Any exercise that causes the back to curve excessively especially with an added load should be modified or avoided.
claim: Osteoporosis: modify or avoid sustained, repeated or end-range spinal flexion and loaded excessive back rounding; teach a hip hinge instead of banning lifting.

quote: For all people with osteoarthritis, offer therapeutic exercise tailored to their needs (for example, local muscle strengthening, general aerobic fitness).
claim: Osteoarthritis: tailored therapeutic exercise (local strengthening plus general aerobic fitness) is a core treatment for everyone with OA.

quote: Advise people with osteoarthritis that joint pain may increase when they start therapeutic exercise. Explain that: doing regular and consistent exercise, even though this may initially cause pain or discomfort, will be beneficial for their joints
claim: Warn people with OA that joint pain may rise when they start exercising and that regular exercise still benefits their joints.

quote: Exclude specific causes of low back pain, for example, cancer, infection, trauma or inflammatory disease such as spondyloarthritis.
claim: Low back pain care starts with clinicians excluding specific causes (cancer, infection, trauma, inflammatory disease); new or changed symptoms need clinical review.
population: people aged 16+ with low back pain

quote: information on the nature of low back pain and sciatica encouragement to continue with normal activities. [2016] Exercise 1.2.2 Consider a group exercise programme (biomechanical, aerobic, mind–body or a combination of approaches)
claim: Low back pain: encourage continuing normal activities; exercise programmes (strengthening, aerobic, mind-body or combined) are recommended, chosen by preference and capability.
population: people aged 16+ with low back pain

quote: research increasingly indicates that resistance training can offer unique benefits for children and adolescents when appropriately prescribed and supervised
claim: NSCA position statement: resistance training can offer unique benefits for children and adolescents when it is appropriately prescribed and supervised.
used_for: youth resistance training: consensus support for supervised training
caveat: Abstract only; it does not give loads, sets or frequency.

quote: many of the benefits associated with adult resistance training programs are attainable by children and adolescents who follow age-specific resistance training guidelines
claim: NSCA: many of the benefits of adult resistance training are attainable by children and adolescents who follow age-specific resistance-training guidelines, so youth programmes are not copies of adult programmes.
population: children and adolescents (adolescence defined as girls 12-18 and boys 14-18 years)
caveat: Abstract only; the age-specific guidelines themselves are not in the saved text.

quote: The majority of youth resistance training injuries are the result of accidents that are potentially preventable with increased supervision and stricter safety guidelines.
claim: In US emergency-room records, most youth resistance-training injuries were accidents (for example dropped weights or improper equipment use) that are potentially preventable with more supervision and stricter safety guidelines.
population: US emergency-room patients aged 8-30; youth means 8-18 years
caveat: Emergency-room visits only, 2002-2005; no exposure data, so it gives no injury rate per hour of training. In the 8-13 group two thirds of injuries were to the hand and foot (dropping and pinching).

quote: Secular declines in measures of muscular fitness in modern-day youth highlight the need for participation in youth resistance training for nonathletes as well as athletes.
claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics (2020) says declining muscular fitness in youth highlights the need for resistance training for nonathletes as well as athletes.
population: children and adolescents, athletes and nonathletes
used_for: youth resistance training: current paediatric policy
caveat: Abstract only; the report's loads, volume and supervision details were not accessible.

quote: countering muscle disuse through resistance training is a powerful intervention to combat the loss of muscle strength and muscle mass, physiological vulnerability, and their debilitating consequences on physical functioning, mobility, independence
claim: NSCA position statement: resistance training is a powerful intervention against loss of muscle strength and mass in older adults and their consequences for function, mobility and independence.
caveat: Abstract only; program-design numbers are in Izquierdo2021 (POP-22, POP-23).

quote: The revised recommendations include 4 overarching principles and 11 recommendations on PA and SB including inter alia PA promotion as standard care
claim: EULAR 2025 update: physical activity promotion should be standard care for people with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis; the recommendations also cover measuring activity, intervention modalities, dose and behaviour change techniques.
population: people with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis
used_for: OA: physical activity as standard care
caveat: Abstract only; the dose details of the 11 recommendations are not in the saved text.

quote: initial prescription should use low volume (1–2 sets) and low-moderate training intensities (≤60% 1 RM)
claim: Youth without resistance-training experience start with low volume and low-to-moderate intensity.
population: youth (children and adolescents) in supervised resistance training

quote: Once basic exercise technique is competent, then prescription should be progressed; for example, 2–4 sets of 6–12 repetitions with a low-moderate training intensity (≤80% 1 RM)
claim: Once technique is competent, progress youth to about 2-4 sets of 6-12 repetitions at low-to-moderate intensity.
population: youth (children and adolescents) in supervised resistance training

quote: youth can be introduced to periodic phases of lower repetition ranges (≤6) and higher external loads (>85% 1 RM) in training, on the proviso that technical competency remains
claim: With more training age, youth can have periodic phases of heavier loads and lower repetitions, provided technique holds.
population: youth (children and adolescents) in supervised resistance training

quote: 2–3 sessions per week on non-consecutive days is most appropriate
claim: Youth resistance training: 2-3 sessions per week on non-consecutive days.
population: youth (children and adolescents) in supervised resistance training

quote: rest periods of approximately 1 min should suffice for most children. However, this may need to be increased (eg, 2–3 min) as the intensity of training increases
claim: Rest about 1 min between sets for most children, longer (2-3 min) as intensity and skill demands rise.
population: youth (children and adolescents) in supervised resistance training
